title: Agent Coders Clinic
text:
0.1 What is the Agent Coders Clinic?
The Agent Coders Clinic is a hands-on workshop where you’ll learn to use AI coding agents — tools that can read your files, run commands, edit code, and work through multi-step tasks on your behalf. Whether this is your first time using an AI coding tool or you’ve been experimenting on your own, this clinic will give you a practical workflow you can take back to your daily work.

title: Agent Coders Clinic
text:
0.2 What you’ll learn
By the end of this clinic, you will:

Understand what an agentic coding harness is and how it differs from chatbots or autocomplete
Connect to a shared gateway that gives you access to Claude and open-source models — no accounts or subscriptions needed
Practice a clear–handoff–notes workflow that keeps your work organized across sessions
Try a group activity where an agent analyzes a real GitHub repository
Learn how to write SKILLS.md files that teach an agent reusable tasks

title: Agent Coders Clinic
text:
0.3 The environment
Everything runs on a sandboxed JupyterHub. You have a terminal, a file browser, and your choice of coding tool. Nothing connects to private or confidential systems — this is a safe space for learning and experimenting.

title: Agent Coders Clinic
text:
0.5 Ready?
Start with Setup & Connection to get your tools connected.

title: 2  Setup & Connection
text:
2.1 What you need
Two things from the organizer:
Your key has its own spending limit and expiry date. Keep it to yourself.

title: 2  Setup & Connection
text:
Gateway URL — the address of the shared gateway
Personal key — starts with sk-, sent to you privately

title: 2  Setup & Connection
text:
2.2 Set your environment variables
In a terminal, run:
export GATEWAY_KEY=sk-your-key-here
export GATEWAY_URL=https://your-gateway-url-here
These last only for this terminal session. If you open a new terminal, run both lines again.

title: 2  Setup & Connection
text:
2.3 Connect your tool
Pick the tool you want to use. You only need one.

2.3.1 Claude Code
Install (if you don’t have it):
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
Connect to the gateway:
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=$GATEWAY_URL
export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=$GATEWAY_KEY
export ANTHROPIC_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5-20251001
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL=claude-opus-4-6
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL=claude-sonnet-4-6
export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5-20251001
If you normally use Claude Code another way (Bedrock, Vertex, or an Anthropic API key), clear those settings so they don’t override the gateway:
unset CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
Start with claude. Type /status to confirm the gateway URL. /model switches models.


2.3.2 OpenCode
Install (if you don’t have it):
npm install -g opencode-ai
Write the config file (this replaces any existing ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json — save a copy first if you have one):
mkdir -p ~/.config/opencode
cat > ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json <<EOF
{
  "\$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "model": "gateway/claude-haiku-4-5-20251001",
  "small_model": "gateway/claude-haiku-4-5-20251001",
  "provider": {
    "gateway": {
      "npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible",
      "name": "Workshop gateway",
      "options": {
        "baseURL": "$GATEWAY_URL/v1",
        "apiKey": "{env:GATEWAY_KEY}"
      },
      "models": {
        "claude-haiku-4-5-20251001": {},
        "claude-sonnet-4-6": {},
        "claude-opus-4-6": {},
        "qwen3-coder-480b": {},
        "qwen3-coder-30b": {},
        "devstral-2": {},
        "kimi-k2.5": {},
        "glm-5": {},
        "minimax-m2.5": {},
        "deepseek-v3.2": {},
        "gpt-oss-120b": {}
      }
    }
  }
}
EOF
Start with opencode. The gateway models are under “Workshop gateway” in /models.


2.3.3 GitHub Copilot CLI
Install (if you don’t have it):
curl -fsSL https://gh.io/copilot-install | bash
Connect to the gateway:
export COPILOT_PROVIDER_TYPE=openai
export COPILOT_PROVIDER_BASE_URL=$GATEWAY_URL/v1
export COPILOT_PROVIDER_API_KEY=$GATEWAY_KEY
export COPILOT_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5-20251001
Start with copilot. To switch models, quit, change COPILOT_MODEL, and restart.

title: 2  Setup & Connection
text:
2.4 Verify it works
Once your tool is running, try a simple prompt:

What directory am I in? List the files here.

If the agent reads your filesystem and responds, you’re connected.

title: 3  Models & Budget
text:
3.2 When to switch models

Haiku — your everyday model. Use it for most tasks.
Sonnet or Opus — reach for these when Haiku struggles: complex reasoning, large refactors, subtle bugs. Switch back when you’re done.
Open models — interesting to try, but they use file-reading and editing tools less reliably than Claude. If one answers without looking at your files, ask it explicitly (e.g., “use the read tool on notes.txt”).

title: 3  Models & Budget
text:
3.3 Switching models

Claude Code: /model claude-sonnet-4-6 (or any model name from the table)
OpenCode: /models, then select from the list
Copilot CLI: quit, change COPILOT_MODEL, restart

title: 3  Models & Budget
text:
3.4 Checking your budget
Run this in a terminal (with GATEWAY_URL and GATEWAY_KEY set):
curl -s $GATEWAY_URL/key/info \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GATEWAY_KEY" |
  python3 -c "
import sys, json
i = json.load(sys.stdin)['info']
print(f\"Spent \${i['spend']:.2f} of \${i['max_budget']:.2f}; expires {i['expires'][:10]}\")
"
Spending shows up about a minute after each request.

title: 3  Models & Budget
text:
3.5 Making your budget last

Stay on Haiku for routine tasks. It’s the best cost-to-capability ratio.
Switch to Sonnet/Opus only when you need to, then switch back.
Use /clear between tasks — this resets the conversation, which means the agent sends less context with each request and each request costs less.
The gateway caches repeated context for Claude models, so later requests in a session cost less than the first one.







Tip



Running /usage in Claude Code shows what the current session has spent.

title: 4  What Is Agentic Coding?
text:
4.1 The idea
You’ve probably used AI chat — you type a question, you get an answer. Maybe you’ve used autocomplete in an editor, where an AI suggests the next few characters as you type.
An agentic coding tool is different. It’s a program — sometimes called an agentic harness — that gives an AI model access to your actual development environment: your files, your terminal, and your git repository. Instead of just answering questions, it can:

title: 4  What Is Agentic Coding?
text:
Read your files to understand your project
Search across your codebase for patterns or definitions
Edit files directly
Run commands in your terminal (with your permission)
Iterate — check its own work, fix mistakes, and keep going

title: 4  What Is Agentic Coding?
text:
4.2 The agent loop
When you give an agentic tool a task, it doesn’t just generate text. It runs a loop:

Think about what to do next
Act — read a file, run a command, make an edit
Observe the result
Repeat until the task is done (or it gets stuck and asks you)

This is why they’re called “agentic” — the model is acting on your behalf, making decisions about what tools to use and in what order.

title: 4  What Is Agentic Coding?
text:
4.3 Examples of agentic harnesses
There are several tools that work this way. In this clinic you can use any of them through the shared gateway:

Claude Code — Anthropic’s CLI tool, built for Claude
OpenCode — open-source, works with Claude and open models
GitHub Copilot CLI — GitHub’s coding tool
Gemini CLI — Google’s coding tool

They all follow the same basic pattern: you give a prompt, the agent works through it using tools, and you review the result. The commands and interface differ, but the concept is the same.

title: 4  What Is Agentic Coding?
section: 4.4 What makes this useful for science?
text:
4.4 What makes this useful for science?

Exploring unfamiliar code — point the agent at a repo and ask “what does this do?” It will actually read the files, not guess.
Repetitive tasks — reformatting data, updating documentation, running the same analysis across multiple files.
Learning — ask the agent to explain code as it works. It’s like pair programming with a patient partner.
Reproducibility — the agent can check whether a project has the dependencies, data, and instructions someone else would need to reproduce it.

title: 4  What Is Agentic Coding?
text:
4.5 What it’s not

It’s not magic — agents make mistakes, especially on complex or ambiguous tasks.
It’s not a replacement for understanding your own code — always review what the agent produces.
It doesn’t remember between sessions — more on that in Agent Skills 101.

title: 5  Activity: Repo Reproducibility Analysis
text:
5.1 The task
In this group activity, you’ll point an AI coding agent at a public GitHub repository and ask it to analyze how reproducible the project is.
This is a great first task for an agentic tool because it’s read-only (nothing to break), it exercises the agent’s ability to explore files, and it produces something useful.

title: 5  Activity: Repo Reproducibility Analysis
text:
5.2 Instructions

5.2.1 1. Pick a repository
Choose a public GitHub repo — it could be:

A repo from your own work or team
A paper’s companion repository
Any open-source scientific project

Clone it into your workspace:
git clone https://github.com/owner/repo-name.git
cd repo-name


5.2.2 2. Start your agent
Launch your coding tool in the cloned repo directory. For example:
claude


5.2.3 3. Ask it to analyze reproducibility
Try a prompt like:

Analyze this repository for reproducibility. Check whether it has:

A README with clear instructions for running the code
Dependency management (requirements.txt, environment.yml, renv.lock, etc.)
Data availability (included, linked, or instructions to obtain)
A clear entry point (what do you run first?)
Any hardcoded paths or system-specific assumptions

Summarize what’s good and what’s missing.



5.2.4 4. Follow up
Once the agent gives its analysis, dig deeper:

“What would someone need to install to run this?”
“Are there any files that reference paths that wouldn’t exist on another machine?”
“Could you write a checklist of what’s needed to make this fully reproducible?”



5.2.5 5. Save your findings
Ask the agent to save its analysis:

Save your reproducibility analysis to notes/reproducibility-analysis.md

title: 5  Activity: Repo Reproducibility Analysis
text:
5.3 Discussion
After the activity, consider:

Did the agent find things you would have missed on a quick scan?
Did it get anything wrong?
How would you improve the prompt if you did this again?







Tip



This kind of task — read-only exploration and analysis — is one of the safest and most effective ways to use an agentic tool. The agent can read every file in a repo in seconds, something that would take a person much longer.

title: 6  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
text:
6.1 The problem
AI coding agents don’t remember anything between sessions. When you start a new session — or run /clear — the agent has no idea what you were doing five minutes ago. It starts fresh every time.
You might think the solution is to build up a huge memory file that the agent loads at the start of every session. But that creates its own problems: the file gets long, stale, and full of context the agent doesn’t need for the current task. It wastes budget re-reading old information.
There’s a simpler approach.
crumbs: 6  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: 6  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
text:
6.2 The workflow: clear, handoff, notes
The core habit is three steps:

6.2.1 1. Work on a task
Start your agent and give it something to do. As it works, it builds up conversation context — the files it has read, the decisions it has made, the changes it has written.


6.2.2 2. Before you stop: handoff
When you’re done with a task (or switching to something else), tell the agent:

Write a handoff note to notes/ summarizing what you did, what’s left, and any decisions you made.

The agent creates a short file — like notes/handoff-2026-09-29.md — capturing exactly what the next session needs to know.


6.2.3 3. Clear and continue
Run /clear (or close the session). The conversation context is gone, but the handoff note is on disk.
Next time, start the agent and say:

Read the notes in notes/ and pick up where we left off.

The agent reads the handoff, gets oriented, and continues the work.
crumbs: 6  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: 6  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
section: 6.3 What goes in a handoff note
text:
6.3 What goes in a handoff note
Good handoff notes are short and specific:

What was done (in a sentence or two)
What’s next (the immediate next step)
Any decisions made that aren’t obvious from the code
Blockers or open questions
crumbs: 6  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: 6  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
section: 6.4 What does NOT go in a handoff note
text:
6.4 What does NOT go in a handoff note

Entire file contents — the agent can read files itself
Code dumps — the code is in the repo
Full project history — keep it to what’s relevant right now
Anything the agent can figure out by looking at the repo







Tip



Think of a handoff note like a sticky note for a colleague: “I finished X, next step is Y, watch out for Z.”
crumbs: 6  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: 6  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
text:
6.5 Example
Here’s what a handoff note might look like:
# Handoff — 2026-09-29

## Done
- Set up Quarto book structure for clinic docs
- Wrote first drafts of setup and models chapters

## Next
- Write the "What Is Agentic Coding?" chapter
- Review setup chapter against latest participant-quickstart.md

## Decisions
- Dropped PDF/docx output for now — HTML only until content stabilizes
- Using parts in _quarto.yml to group chapters into sections
crumbs: 6  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: 6  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
text:
6.6 Why /clear matters
Every message you send includes the entire conversation so far. As the conversation grows, each request sends more tokens and costs more. Running /clear resets this — your next request is cheap again.
The handoff note means you don’t lose anything important. You trade a long, expensive conversation for a short, focused one with a lightweight file to get the agent back up to speed.
crumbs: 6  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: 6  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
text:
6.7 The notes/ directory
Keep handoff notes and working notes in a notes/ directory in your project. This keeps them separate from your actual project files and easy to find.
Some things that work well in notes/:

Handoff notes (handoff-YYYY-MM-DD.md)
Plans and task lists for ongoing work
Analysis summaries from agent tasks (like the reproducibility analysis)
crumbs: 6  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: 6  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
text:
6.8 Branches and PRs
Once you’re comfortable with clear/handoff/notes, you can add git branches and pull requests to the workflow:

Create a branch for a task
Do the work (with clear/handoff as needed)
Open a PR when it’s ready
Merge and move on

This is a natural complement — the branch keeps your changes isolated and reviewable, and the handoff notes help you (or someone else) pick up the work if it spans multiple sessions. But the clear/handoff/notes habit is the foundation. Get that down first.
crumbs: 6  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: 7  Agent Skills 102: SKILLS.md
text:
7.1 What is SKILLS.md?
A SKILLS.md file lives in your project and teaches the agent reusable tasks — things you do repeatedly that you want done the same way every time. Instead of re-explaining a process in every session, you write it once in SKILLS.md and the agent follows it.
Think of it as a recipe book for your agent.

title: 7  Agent Skills 102: SKILLS.md
text:
7.2 How it works
When you tell an agent to use a skill, it reads SKILLS.md, finds the matching section, and follows those instructions. For example:

Use the “render-check” skill to build and verify the book.

The agent looks up “render-check” in SKILLS.md and executes the steps.

title: 7  Agent Skills 102: SKILLS.md
text:
7.3 Writing a skill
A skill is a section in SKILLS.md with a clear name and step-by-step instructions. Keep them concrete and specific.

7.3.1 Example: render-check
## render-check

Render the Quarto book and check for problems.

1. Run `quarto render` in the project root
2. Check the output for errors or warnings
3. If there are errors, read the error message and fix the issue
4. Re-render until it builds cleanly
5. Report what you fixed (if anything)


7.3.2 Example: format-bib
## format-bib

Clean up the bibliography file.

1. Read `content/references.bib`
2. Check each entry for:
   - Missing fields (author, title, year, journal/publisher)
   - Inconsistent formatting (e.g., mixed use of curly braces)
   - Duplicate entries (same DOI or matching author+title+year)
3. Fix any issues found
4. Sort entries alphabetically by citation key


7.3.3 Example: daily-handoff
## daily-handoff

Write an end-of-session handoff note.

1. Summarize what was done in this session
2. List what should happen next
3. Note any decisions or blockers
4. Save to `notes/handoff-YYYY-MM-DD.md` using today's date

title: 7  Agent Skills 102: SKILLS.md
text:
7.4 Tips for writing skills

Be specific. “Check for problems” is vague. “Run quarto render and check for errors” is actionable.
Use numbered steps. The agent follows them in order.
Include the actual commands. Don’t make the agent guess what to run.
Keep them short. A skill that’s a full page long is probably two skills.
Name them clearly. You’ll invoke them by name.

title: 7  Agent Skills 102: SKILLS.md
text:
7.5 Where to put SKILLS.md
Put it in the root of your project, next to CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md. The agent will find it when it reads your project files.

title: 7  Agent Skills 102: SKILLS.md
text:
7.6 SKILLS.md vs. CLAUDE.md









CLAUDE.md
SKILLS.md




Purpose
Project context and conventions
Reusable task recipes


When it’s read
Automatically at session start
When you invoke a skill


Contents
Build commands, architecture, coding style
Step-by-step procedures



Both are useful. CLAUDE.md gives the agent background knowledge. SKILLS.md gives it specific procedures to follow on demand.

title: 8  Tool Comparison
text:
8.2 Key differences
Claude Code is the most full-featured for this clinic. It has built-in commands for managing context (/clear), checking status (/status, /usage), and switching models (/model). It’s designed around Claude and works well with CLAUDE.md project files.
OpenCode is open-source and has the most flexible model configuration. It works well with both Claude and open models through the gateway. Good if you want to compare models side by side.
GitHub Copilot CLI is straightforward to set up. To switch models you need to quit and restart with a different COPILOT_MODEL environment variable. No GitHub account needed when using the gateway.
Gemini CLI is Google’s tool. It follows the same agentic pattern. Configuration is via environment variables.

title: 8  Tool Comparison
text:
8.3 Common commands across tools
Regardless of which tool you use, you’ll do the same basic things:

Give a prompt — type what you want the agent to do
Approve tool use — most tools ask permission before editing files or running commands
Review output — always check what the agent did before moving on
End the session — close the tool or clear context when switching tasks

title: 9  Troubleshooting
text: 9.1 Connection problems

title: 9  Troubleshooting
text:
9.1.1 “Authentication error” or “Invalid API key”
Your GATEWAY_KEY is wrong or not set in this terminal.
echo $GATEWAY_KEY
If it’s empty, set it again:
export GATEWAY_KEY=sk-your-key-here


9.1.2 “Connection refused” or timeout
The gateway server may be stopped. Check with the organizer.
Also verify your GATEWAY_URL is set:
echo $GATEWAY_URL


9.1.3 Claude Code ignores the gateway
If you have other Claude Code settings (Bedrock, Vertex, or an Anthropic API key), they can override the gateway. Clear them:
unset CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
Then set the gateway variables again and restart claude.

title: 9  Troubleshooting
text:
9.2 Budget problems

9.2.1 “Budget exceeded”
Your key has hit its spending limit. Ask the organizer — they can increase it or issue a new key.


9.2.2 “Key expired” or “Key blocked”
The key’s time limit is up, or it was switched off. Ask the organizer for a new one.


9.2.3 How to check your remaining budget
curl -s $GATEWAY_URL/key/info \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GATEWAY_KEY" |
  python3 -c "
import sys, json
i = json.load(sys.stdin)['info']
print(f\"Spent \${i['spend']:.2f} of \${i['max_budget']:.2f}; expires {i['expires'][:10]}\")
"

title: 9  Troubleshooting
text:
9.3 Agent behavior problems

9.3.1 Agent gives generic answers without reading files
Some models (especially open models) don’t use file-reading tools reliably. Try:

Being explicit: “Use the read tool to look at README.md, then answer.”
Switching to a Claude model, which handles tool use more reliably.



9.3.2 Agent seems confused or stuck
The conversation may have gotten too long. Run /clear and start fresh. If you have handoff notes in notes/, tell the agent to read those for context.


9.3.3 Agent makes changes you didn’t ask for
Review what the agent is doing before approving. Most tools ask permission before writing files. If it’s going off track, interrupt it and clarify what you actually want.

title: 9  Troubleshooting
text:
9.4 Environment variables cheat sheet
If things aren’t working, check that all the right variables are set:
echo "GATEWAY_URL: $GATEWAY_URL"
echo "GATEWAY_KEY: $GATEWAY_KEY"
echo "ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL: $ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL"
echo "ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN: $ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN"
echo "ANTHROPIC_MODEL: $ANTHROPIC_MODEL"
For Claude Code, ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL should match GATEWAY_URL and ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN should match GATEWAY_KEY.
